full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J: This Civil Appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 5-7-2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4041 of 1999 making the rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree dated 14-9-1999 passed by the Additional District Judge, Bagerhat in Title Appeal No. 282 of 1994 affirming the judgment and decree dated 6-10-1994 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Bagerhat in Title Suit No.225 of 1994 decreeing the suit.

<u>2. The appellant, as plaintiff, filed Title Suit No. 13 of 1993 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Bagerhat, which was subsequently transferred to the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Bagerhat and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 225 of 1994, for declaration of title in respect of 5.09 acres of land and for further declaration that the compromise decree passed in Title Suit No.173 of 1994, by the learned Subordinate Judge, Khulna is fraudulent, inoperative, void and not binding upon the plaintiff and also for further declaration that the enlistment of the suit land in the list of vested and non-resident property is not binding upon the plaintiff and for permanent injunction.</u>

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the land measuring 6.05 acres appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.152 of No. 3 Nalbaria Mouza originally belonged to Ganga Charan. Ganga Charan settled the said land to Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader by registered patta dated 24-3-1936. Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader subsequently transferred the said land to Burundi Hawlader the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 44-60 by a registered kabala dated 27-8-1943. Burundi Hawlader died leaving behind the defendant Nos. 44-60 as his heirs. That the defendant Nos. 44-60 transferred 5.09 acres, of land out of that 6.05 acres of land to the plaintiff by a registered kabala dated 28-1-1993 and also delivered possession of the said land in favour of the plaintiff and since then the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land. Further case of the plaintiff is that at the time of RS operation the suit land was recorded in the name of Shashi Kumar Singh and Jogesh Chandra Shil wrongly. That Burundi Hawlader died just before RS operation and his heirs-the defendant Nos. 44-60 had no other capable man to look after the property and taking that opportunity Jogesh Chandra Shil-the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 42 and 43 managed to record 4.36 acres of land of plot No. 2174 and 0.96 acre of land of plot No.796 of RS Khatian No. 791 in his name. Thereafter, at the time of SA.operation also the said land was recorded in the name of Jogesh Chandra Shil in SA Khatian Nos. 1114 and 1032. That although the suit land was recorded in RS and SA Khatians in the name of Jogesh Chandra Shil, but he had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. That the plaintiff has been possessing the suit-land and before him the heirs of Burundi Hawlader possessed the suit land. That due to erroneous recording of the suit land in RS and SA Khatians the plaintiff's title in the suit land has been clouded and hence the suit.

4. The defendant Nos. 1, 7, 9, 11, 12-14, 20, 23, 25, 26(Ka)-26(Cha), 27, 28, 32-34, 36 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the case of the plaintiff. The material case of these contesting defendants is that the suit land originally belonged to Shashi Kumar Singh under the landlord Satya Charan Saha and Korman Akon. That while owning and possessing the suit land Shashi Kumar Singh settled the suit land along with other lands to the predecessor-in-interest of these contesting defendants on 1st Baishakh, 1355 BS at a rent of Taka 315 and delivered possession. That in pursuance of that settlement.the landlord executed an amalnama on 1st Ashar, 1355 BS and also granted dakhilas in favour of the defendants and their predecessors-in-interest. At the time of SA operation the suit land was erroneously recorded in the name of the original owner Shashi Kumar Singh in Khatian No. 1114. That Shashi Kumar Singh died leaving behind 2 sons, namely, Kanailal Singh and Hiralal Singh. These defendants brought Title Suit No. 173 of 1964 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna against Kanailal Singh and Hiralal Singh and that suit was decreed on compromise on 8-9-1964. That on the basis of erroneous record of fight the local tahshilder claimed the suit land as vested and non- resident property and denied to receive rent of the suit land and then the defendants brought Title Suit No. 109 of 1971 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Khulna for declaration of their title and for further declaration that the enlistment of the suit land in the list of vested and non-resident property was void. That suit was decreed on 15-6-1972. Thereafter, the officials of the vested and non-resident property, in collusion with the local enemies of these defendants, threatened the defendants to dispossess them from the suit land and, as such, the defendants brought Title Suit No.207 of 1978 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Bagerhat for permanent injunction and obtained decree on 20-12-1980. Against the said judgment and decree the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Bagerhat and Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Sharankhola brought Title Suit No. 33 of 1985 for setting aside the said decree and that suit was dismissed on 8-6-1991. That the plaintiff has/had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. The defendant Nos. 37-41 (government officials) also contested the suit by filing written statements. The material case of these defendants is that the SA recorded landlord Mohadeb Singh brought rent suit against the tenant for non-payment of rent and obtained decree and took the suit land in his khas possession after purchasing the same in auction in Rent Execution Case No.2603 of 1941 arising out of Rent Suit No. 908 of 1941. At the time of RS operation the suit land was recorded in the name of Shashi Kumar Singh, son of Mohadeb Singh. Accordingly SA record of right also was prepared in the name of Shashi Kumar Singh. That Shashi Kumar Singh left this country for India before 1965 and, as such, the suit land was enlisted as enemy property. Neither the plaintiff nor the other defendants have had any right, title and possession in the suit land. That the suit is liable to be dismissed and the decree passed in Title Suit No. 173 of 1964 also is liable to be declared void.

6. The trial court, on consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties, decreed the suit. The appellate court below also affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. The High Court Division reversed the concurrent findings and decision of the trial court and the appellate court below and dismissed the suit making observations to the effect that the suit is barred by limitation. The High Court Division did not believe also the plaintiff's case and made observations to the effect that the Exhibit-6(sale certificate) has been supported by other documents together with several decrees of the competent court all of which tell against the case of the plaintiff.

7. Leave was granted to consider the submissions of the learned Counsel of the plaintiff-leave-petitioner to the effect that the High Court Division was wrong in making the rule absolute ignoring the concurrent findings and decision of the courts of facts relying on Exhibit-6 and other so-called decrees which were not at all binding upon the plaintiff; that the High Court Division, on misconception of law, failed to appreciate the so-called Exhibit-6 in its true purport, that the alleged sale certificate having not been substantiated by sale proclamation and writ of delivery of possession the alleged auction purchase was not established to have taken effect; that the High Court Division was wrong in finding the suit barred by limitation on misconception of law inasmuch as it is well settled that if the plaintiff comes with a suit for declaration that the entry made in the records of right is wrong, in that case Article 120 of the Limitation Act will be applicable, but the plaintiff is not bound to institute a suit for declaration that the entry is wrong, he can wait and when an invasion on his rights is made on the basis of wrong entry, he can sue for a declaration of his title on the ground that the record is wrong and, as such, the instant suit brought within 6 years from the date of threatened invasion is well within, time.

8. We have heard Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant and Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Senior Advocate for the respondent Nos. 3-22 and Mr Pari mal Chandra Guha, the learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 46 and 47-sons of Jogesh Chandra Shil. It should be mentioned here that these respondent Nos. 46 and 47 who were the defendant Nos. 42 and 43 in the original suit though did not contest in the trial court or appellate court below or in the High Court Division, but in this Division they, for the first time, have appeared and have submitted an additional paper book stating to the effect that they did not receive any notice of the original suit and, as such, could not contest the same, that they are recorded owners in possession of 0.79 acre out of the suit land. That the suit land belonged to Ganga Charan under landlord Mohadeb Singh who died leaving only son Shashi Kumai Singh. That the suit land was sold in auction for arrears of rent in Rent Suit No. 2603 of 1941 which was purchased by Shashi Kumar Singh on 17-1-1941, and delivery of possession was taken by him in Rent Execution Case No. 908 of 1941 and the sale certificate was confirmed on 20-1-1994. That Shashi Kumar Singh settled 2.96 acres of land to Jogesh Chandra Shil on 28th Chaitra 1347 BS Jogesh Chandra Shil possessed that land and RS Khatian and SA Khatian were prepared in his name rightly. Jogesh Chandra Shil subsequently died leaving two sons the respondent Nos. 46 and 47 and these respondent Nos. 46 and 47 have been possessing this land. That the plaintiff has got no right, title and possession in this land.

9. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellant has mainly argued to the effect that it is an admitted fact that Ganga Charan was the CS recorded owner of the suit land; that the plaintiff has proved his case that this Ganga Charan settled the suit land to Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader by registered patta dated 24-3-1936 the Exhibit-5 and subsequently Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader sold the suit land to Burundi Hawlader by a registered kabala dated 27-8-1943 the Exhibit-5(Ka) and the heirs of Burundi Hawlader-the defendant Nos.44-60 subsequently, sold the suit land to the plaintiff by a registered deed dated 28-1-1993 the Exhibit-1. The learned Counsel has argued that all these above documents including the CS record of the suit land in the name of Ganga Charan sufficiently prove the plaintiff's case that he has acquired the suit land from its rightful owners. The learned Counsel has argued that though the contesting defendants have claimed that the suit land was sold in auction and Shashi Kumar Singh purchased the same in auction, but this alleged auction purchase of the suit land by Shashi Kumar Singh has not been proved at all. The learned Counsel has argued that so-called sale certificate the Exhibit-6 cannot, be relied on at all since this Exhibit-6 has not been substantiated by sale proclamation and writ of delivery of possession. The learned Counsel has argued that the appellate court below rightly did not put any reliance on this Exhibit-6, but the High Court Division dismissed the suit of the plaintiff most illegally relying on this Exhibit-6-the sale certificate which is not acceptable at all. The learned Counsel has argued also that the decisions of the courts off acts being founded on concurrent findings of fact the High Court Division in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure committed illegality in setting aside the concurrent findings and decision of the courts of facts without assigning any cogent reasonund. The learned Counsel has argued also that in none of the previous suits as alleged by the contesting defendants the predecessors of the plaintiff were made parties and, as such, the plaintiff is not bound by those decrees. The learned Counsel has contended that all those decrees were obtained collusively by practicing fraud upon the courts. The learned Counsel has argued also that in none of the earlier suits there has been any adjudication as to the title of the property in question and, as such, the decrees passed in those suits will not operate as res-judicata in the present suit. Mr Mahmudul Islam has argued also that the High Court Division was wrong in finding the suit as barred by limitation, that the plaintiff being in possession of the suit land has filed the suit for declaration of title, and, as such, the suit cannot be held as barred by limitation. The learned Counsel has contended that had it been a suit for declaration that the entry made in the record of right is wrong, in that case Article 120 of the Limitation Act would have been applicable, but the present suit is for declaration of title and it has been instituted when the defendants made an attempt to invade on plaintiff’s right on the basis of the wrong entry and, as such, this suit is well within time.

10. Mr Mahmudul Islam has made argument also countering the case of the respondent Nos. 46 and 47 by pointing out that according to the case of these defendants Shashi Kumar Singh acquired the suit land by virtue of auction sale dated 7-11-1941 but they claimed that their predecessor Jogesh Chandra Shil got settlement of the suit land from Shashi Kumar Singh on 12-4-1941 which is absurd.

11. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Counsel for the respondent Nos. 3 to 22 has made submissions supporting the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. The learned Counsel has made argument to the effect that in this suit the plaintiff has totally failed to prove his right, title and possession in the suit land and in the circumstances the High Court Division rightly dismissed the suit. The learned Counsel has argued also that though the plaintiff has claimed that Ganga Charan the original owner of the suit land settled the suit land to Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader by registered patta 24-3-1936 and that subsequently, Ananta Kumar Nittananda Hawlader transferred the same to Hawlader the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 44 to 60 by a registered deed dated 27- 8-1943 and have produced the certified copy of the two transfer deeds only, but could not adduce any other evidence whatsoever to prove that these two registered deeds were actually acted upon and that Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader possessed the suit land and thereafter, Burundi Hawlader possessed the suit land and after the death of Burundi Hawlader his heirs-the defendant Nos. 44 to 60 possessed the suit land and the plaintiff by so-called purchase from the defendant Nos. 44 to 60 got possession of the suit land and possessed the same. The learned Counsel has pointed out that admittedly the suit land was not recorded in the name of these alleged predecessors of the plaintiff in any of the records of right and there is no evidence at all to prove that they ever paid any rent for the suit land. The learned Advocate has argued that the witnesses whom the plaintiff adduced to support his case are not reliable and dependable witnesses at all and they also could not prove plaintiff's or his alleged predecessors possession in the suit land at all. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali has argued also that there are abundance of evidence on record to prove the contesting defendants' right, title and possession in the suit land and that the High Court Division, on consideration of these evidence of the contesting defendants and the facts and circumstances rightly dismissed the suit of the plaintiff.

12. Mr Parimal Chandra Guha the learned Advocate for the respondent Nos.46 and 47 has frankly admitted that the respondent Nos.46 and 47 though have claimed to have been in possession of certain portion of the suit land, but they have got no documents in support of their title in the suit land.

13. We have considered the submissions of all the learned Advocates and gone through the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and also those of the appellate court below and the trial court.

14. We have also examined the evidence on record.

15. It is not denied that Ganga Charan was the C. S. recorded owner of the suit land. But the contesting defendants specific case is that for arrear of rent the suit land was sold in auction and Shashi Kumar Singh purchased the same on 17 November, 1941 and subsequently Shashi Kumar Singh settled the suit land along with other lands to the predecessors-in-interest of the contesting defendants and since then the predecessors-in- interest of the contesting defendants and thereafter the contesting defendants have been possessing the suit land. To substantiate this case the contesting defendants have filed the sale certificate which has been marked as Exhibit-6. It appears that in the appellate court below, at the instance of the contesting defendants, the relevant register also for proving this sale certificate was called for and it was produced before the appellate court below and the appellate court below examined the same. So, from this sale certificate the Exhibit-6 it appears that the suit land was sold in auction and Shashi Kumar Singh purchased the same. It has been argued from the side of the plaintiff that in the absence of sale proclamation and writ of delivery of possession this sale certificate-the Exhibit-6 alone cannot prove that this sale certificate was acted upon and Shashi Kumar Singh got delivery of possession of the suit land and became the owner of the same. It is true that the sale proclamation and writ of delivery of possession in support of this sale certificate the Exhibit-6 were not produced before the court. But it appears that there are some other strong evidence to substantiate the case of the contesting defendants that Shashi Kumar Singh became owner of the suit land by virtue of the auction purchase and he subsequently settled the same with the predecessors-in-interest of the contesting defendants and since then the predecessors-in-interest of the contesting defendants and the contesting defendants have been possessing the suit land. The contesting defendants filed a suit for partition being Partition Suit No. 173 of 1964 against the sons of Shashi Kumar Singh and got a decree on compromise in the year 1964 from a competent civil court. The contesting defendants filed another suit being Title Suit No. 109 of 1971 for declaration of their title in the suit land and for further declaration that the suit land was not enemy property against the enemy property authority and that suit also was decreed on 15-6-1972. On the basis of this decree dated 15-6-1972 the defendants also got the suit land mutated in their names by filing a Miscellaneous Case being No. 111973-74 under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thereafter, the defendants filed another suit being Title Suit No. 207 of 1978 for permanent injunction against the enemy property authority and others and that suit also was decreed on 20- 12-1980. The Government filed Title Suit No.33 of 1985 for setting aside the decree dated 20-12- 1980 passed in Title Suit No .207 of 1978, but that suit also was dismissed on 33-6-1991. One of the defendants filed Petition Case No. 267 of 1984 under section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code which was also allowed. The contesting defendants have filed the necessary papers of these above stated suits and case to substantiate their case. All these papers along with mutated khatian of the suit land in the name of the contesting defendants strongly supports the defendants case that their predecessors-in-interest acquired the suit land from Shashi Kumar Singh by way of settlement in the year 1355 BS and since then they and after them these contesting defendants have been possessing the suit land.

16. The plaintiff, on the other hand, could not produce a single documentary evidence to prove his or his alleged predecessors possession in the suit land. Save and except certified copies of the patta deed dated 24-3-1936 allegedly executed by Ganga Charan in favour of Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawladerand the transfer deed dated 27-8-1943 allegedly executed by Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader in favour of Burundi Hawlader-the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 44 to 60, the plaintiff could not produce any other single documentary evidence to prove that these two alleged transfer deeds were actually acted upon and the recipients of these deeds got possession of the suit land and they possessed the same also on the basis of these deeds. Admittedly, in none of the RS and SA khatians of the suit land the names of these Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader and Burundi Hawlader were recorded. Not a single rent receipt could be filed by the plaintiff to show that any of these alleged owners of the suit land ever paid rent for the suit land. No other papers also could be filed by the plaintiff to show that these alleged owners of the suit land or even the vendors of the plaintiff ever made any attempt to record the suit land in their names. In the circumstances the above mentioned documentary evidence adduced' by the contesting defendants strongly supports not only the defence case, but also strongly tell against the plaintiff's case. The plaintiff claimed to have purchased the suit land from the defendant Nos. 44 to 60 by registered kabala dated 27-8-1993. Within a few months of this alleged purchase the plaintiff has filed this suit. However, before purchasing the suit land the plaintiff must have enquired about the records of right of the suit land and known that none of the records of right was prepared in the name of his vendors or their predecessors. But in spite of that he purchased the suit land. This fact also tells against the bonafide of the plaintiff.

17. It is true that in none of the previous suits filed by the contesting defendants the plaintiff or his predecessors were made parties. This fact can be a point for argument that the decrees passed in those suits are not binding on the plaintiff or his predecessors. But this fact is of no help for proving the case of the plaintiff. Rather the decrees passed in those suits by competent civil courts strongly support the defendants' case and also strongly tell against the plaintiff's case.

<u>18. It is true that the plaintiff is not bound to institute a suit for declaration that the records of right of the suit land are wrong. It is true that when an invasion on the rights of a person is made on the basis of the wrong records of right he can file a suit for declaration of title and that suit, if brought within 6 years from the date of such invasion, is well within time. But in the present case, as it appears from the above discussion, none of the records of right was prepared in the name of the plaintiff's vendors or his alleged predecessors- in-interest and they never paid rent for the suit land. The plaintiff also purchased the suit land with the knowledge that in none of the records of right, of the suit  and the names of his vendors or their predecessors-in-interest were recorded. The plaintiff could not prove his possession or the possession of his alleged predecessors-in-interest in the suit land by adducing cogent evidence. It appears that the plaintiff has examined 6 witnesses including himself. The PW 1 is the plaintiff himself. The PW 2, in his examination-in-chief, though has stated that the plaintiff possesses the suit land and before that Ananta Kumar, Nittananda Hawlader and Burundi Hawlader possessed the suit land, but during cross-examination this witness has stated that he saw the heirs of Burundi Hawlader to possess the suit land 30/35 years before. The PW 3 though in examination-in- chief has deposed in support of the plaintiff's possession in the suit land, but during cross-examination this witness has stated that Ananta Kumar died two years before and Nittananda Hawlader died four years before and Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader possessed the suit land till their death. He stated "অনন্ত নিত্যানন্দ যতদিন জীবিত ছিলেন ততদিন উক্ত জমি দখল করতেন।" Evidently, this witness is a liar and has deposed falsely. The PW 4 also is not at all a competent person to depose as regards possession of the suit land. During cross- examination this witness has deposed to the effect that he resides 3 miles away from the suit land. During cross-examination this witness has admit- ted also that he is a close relation of the plaintiff and he has got to land in the suit mouza. This witness, during cress-examination, has admitted that he cannot say who possessed the suit land for what period during the last 48/49 years. This witness has stated "মামলার জমি আমি অনুমান ৪৮/৮৯ব ৎসর যাবত চিনি। এই ৪৮/৮৯ বছর ধারাবাহিকভাবে কেক বেদখল করিয়াছে তাহা সব বলিতে পারিনা।" The PW 5 is one of the alleged executants of the plaintiff's kabala and, as such, the most interested witness. During cross-examination this witness has stated that he used to possess the suit land, but he cannot say what quantum of land he possessed. This witness has stated also that there are 2/3 dwelling huts on the suit land. But the PW 2 has stated that there is no hut in the suit land. The PW 6 is a formal witness an employee of registry office who produced a register to prove the certified copy of the patta dated 24-2-1936.</u>

19. From the above discussion, it is evident, that the evidence of the plaintiff's witness could not prove the plaintiff's or his predecessors-in- interest's alleged possession in the suit land at all. It has already been pointed out above that the plaintiff could not produce a single documentary evidence, namely, the khatians or rent receipt in support of his or his alleged predecessors-in-interest's possession in the suit land.

<u>20. In the circumstances the argument that this suit being filed within 6 years from the date of alleged threatened invasion on plaintiff's right on the basis of wrong entry of the suit land in records of right is well within time is not acceptable at all.</u>

<u>21. In this appeal the respondent Nos. 44 and 47 though have claimed right, title and possession in certain portion of the suit land, but admittedly they have no evidence whatsoever in support of their alleged title in the suit land and there is also no evidence on record in support of their alleged possession in their claimed land.</u>

<u>22. However, from the above discussion, it is evident that, in this suit the plaintiff has failed to prove his alleged right, title and possession in the suit land by adducing necessary evidence rather the evidence adduced by the contesting defendants have disproved the case of the plaintiff.</u>

23. In the circumstances we find no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. This appeal, therefore, fails. Hence it is ordered that this appeal be dismissed on contest against the contesting respondents and ex-parte against the rest without any order as to cost.

Syed Mahmud Hossain J : I have had the privilege of going through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my sister Justice Nazmun Ara Sultana. I respectfully differ with the findings, reasonings and decision arrived at by her and propose to deliver an independent judgment giving my own findings, reasonings and decision as under:

This civil appeal, by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 5-7-2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4041 of 1999 making the Rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree dated 14-9-1999 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Bagherhat in Title Appeal No.282 of 1994 affirming the judgment and decree dated 6-10-1994 passed by the then learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Bagherhat in Title Suit No. 225 of 1994 decreeing the suit.

<u>25. The appellant instituted Title Suit No. 225 of 1994 in the Court of the then Subordinate Judge, second Court Bagerhat for declaration of his title in the suit property. His case, in short, is that the land measuring 6.05 acres appertaining to CS khatian No. 152.of No. 3 Nalbunia Mouza under Sharankhola Police Station originally belonged to Ganga Charan. He settled the said land to Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader by a registered patta dated 24-3-1936 who again transferred the said land to Barundi Hawlader, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 44-60 by a registered deed of sale dated 27-8-1943. After that, Barundi Hawlader died leaving behind defendant Nos. 44-60 as his heirs and they transferred 5.09 acres of land (the suit land) out of the said 6.05 acres of land by a registered deed of sale dated 28-1-1993 to the plaintiff and since then the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land. Barundi Hawlader, the predecessor in interest of defendant Nos. 44-60 (vendors of the plaintiff) had died just before RS operation and they had no other capable man to look after the property, and taking that advantage Jogesh Chandra, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant No.42 and 43 in collusion with Shashi Kumar Singh, son of previous landlord Mohadeb Chandra Singh got the suit land recorded partly in the name of Shashi Sekhar and partly in his own name, though none of them had any possession, title and interest in the suit land. The SA records were also prepared wrongly in their names. Such wrong recording has clouded the title of the plain- tiff in the suit land necessitating filing of the suit. Taking advantage of wrong records in respect of the suit land in the name of Shashi Kumar Singh, the predecessors of defendant Nos. 1-10, 11-13, 14-19, 20-26 and 27-36 forging the signatures of Shashi Kumar's sons, Kanai and Hiralal Singh brought Title Suit No. 173 of 1964 on false pleas, and suppressing summons and practicing fraud obtained a compromise decree on 8-8-1964. On the other hand, defendant Nos. 37-40 illegally enlisted the suit property as vested property. They never took over physical possession of the suit property. Defendant Nos. 1-36 and 3 7-40 collusively created obstructions to peaceful possession and enjoyment of the suit property by the plaintiff and hence the title suit has been filed.</u>

26. Defendant Nos. 1, 7, 9, 11-14, 20, 23, 25-28, 30, 32-36 and defendant Nos. 37-41 by filing separate written statements contested the suit. Defendant Nos. 2-4 and 16-19 appeared in the suit by filing a deed of compromise with the plaintiff dated 16-3-1993 and prayed for decree in the terms of the compromise.

27. The case of defendant Nos. 1, 7, 11-14, 20, 23, 25-28, 30, 32-36, in short, is that the suit property originally belonged to Shashi Kumar Singh under the ex-landlord Satya Chandra Saha and Korman Akon. On first Baishakh, 1355 BS Shashi Kumar Singh settled the suit land along with other lands to the predecessor-in-interest of these defendants at a jama of Taka 315 by executing an amalnama on first Asar, 1355 BS and granted dakhilas therefore. At the time of SA operation, the suit land was erroneously recorded in the name of Shashi Kumar Singh in Khatian No. 1114. In the meantime, Shashi Kumar died leaving behind two sons, Kanai Lal Singh and Hira Lal Singh, so the defendant brought Title Suit No. 173 of 1964 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna and on 8-9-1964, the suit was decreed on compromise. On the basis of wrong record of rights, the local Tahsilder claimed the suit land as vested and non-resident property and denied receiving rents. Then the respondents brought Title Suit No. 109 of 1971 in the Court of the then Subordinate Judge, Khulna for declaration of their title together with the declaration that the enlistment of the suit property as vested and non-resident property is void, illegal and the suit was decreed on 15-6-1972. After that, the official/staff of the vested and non-resident property in collusion with the local enemies of the defendants threatened to dispossess them from the suit land. Accordingly, these defendants filed Title Suit No. 207 of 1978 in the Court of the Munsif, First Court, Bagerhat and obtained decree on 20-12-1980. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Bagerhat and TNO, Sharonkhola instituted Title Suit No. 33 of 1985 for setting aside the aforesaid judgment and decree. But their suit was dismissed on 8-6-1991.

28. The case of defendant Nos. 37-41, in short, is that the SA recorded tenant Mahadev Singh brought rent suit against the tenant for non- payment of rent and obtained decree and by filing a rent execution case took the suit land in his khas possession. Rent Execution Case No. 2604 of 1941 arising out of Rent suit No. 908 of 1941 of the First Court of Munsif, Bagerhat was filed. The auction was held on 17-1-1941 and Shashi Kumar Singh purchased the suit land in auction. During RS operation, the suit land was recorded in the name of Shashi Kumar Singh, son of Mahadev Singh. The SA record was prepared in the name of Shashi Kumar Singh who left this country for India before 1965 and accordingly, the suit property was enlisted as enemy property as perstatement of defendant Nos. 37-41. Neither the plaintiff nor other defendants had any right, title and interest in the suit land. These defendants took settlement of the suit land from Shashi Kumar Singh and, as such, the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of Shashi Kumar Singh in order to avoid complications the defendant filed Title Suit No. 173 of 1964 and obtained the compromise decree.

29. The trial Court upon hearing the parties by its judgment and order dated 6-10-1994 decreed the suit. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendants filed Title Appeal No.282 of 1994 before the learned District Judge, Bagerhat. On transfer, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat, who by his judgment and order dated 14-9-1999 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

30. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the appellate Court, the defendants filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 4041 of 1999. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, after hearing the parties, by his judgment and order dated 5-7- 2004 made the Rule absolute without any order as to cost setting aside the judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below.

31. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the plaintiff-leave-petitioner moved this Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 24 of 2005, in which, leave was granted on 25-3-2007, resulting in Civil Appeal No. 46 of 2007.

32. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits as under:

I. Admittedly, Gonga Charan was the CS recorded owner of the suit land and the plaintiff proved his case that Ganga Charan settled the suit land to Ananta Kumar and Nittananda Hawlader by a registered patta dated 24-3-1936, Exhibit-5 and subsequently, Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader sold their under tenancy right to Burundi Hawlader by a registered deed of sale dated 27-8-143, Exhibit 5ka and the heirs of Burundi Hawlader, defendant Nos. 44-60 sold the suit land to the plaintiff by a registered deed of sale dated 28-1-1993, Exhibit-I. And, as such, it has been proved beyond reasonable doubt that the plaintiff acquired title in the suit land.

II. The contesting defendants claimed that the suit land was sold in auction and Shashi Kumer Singh purchased the same but the auction purchase of the suit land by Shashi Kumer Singh was not proved at all.

III. The sale certificate (Exhibit-6) cannot be relied upon since Exhibit-S has not been supported by sale proclamation and writ of delivery of possession.

IV. The appellate Court did not put reliance on Exhibit-6, the sale certificate, and the High Court Division dismissed the suit of the plaintiff solely relying on Exhibit-6, which is not at all tenable in law.

V.In none of the previous suits filed by the, contesting defendants, the predecessors of the plaintiff were made parties and as such, the plaintiff is not bound by those decrees and those decrees were obtained collusively by practicing fraud upon the Courts.

VI. The finding that the suit was barred by limitation was wrong and the plaintiff being in possession of the suit land filed the suit for declaration of title as soon as his right was clouded by the claim of title of the defendants over the suit land.

VII. Respondent Nos. 46 and 47 the alleged heirs of Shashi Kumar Singh could not prove .that their predecessors acquired title and possession in the suit land pursuant to the auction sale dated 7-11-1941.

33. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos. 3-22, on the other hand, submits as under:

I.The plaintiff totally failed to prove his right, title and possession in the suit land and, as such, the High Court Division rightly dismissed the suit.

II. The plaintiff claimed that Gonga Charan the original owner of the suit land, settled the suit land to Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader by a registered patta dated 24-3-1936 and subsequently, Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader transferred their under tenancy right to Burundi Hawlader, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos.44-60 by a registered deed of sale dated 27-8-1943 but could not prove by producing evidence that those two registered deeds were actually acted upon and that Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader possessed the suit land and thereafter, Burundi Hawlader possessed the suit land and after the death of Burundi Hawalder, his heirs, defendant Nos. 44-60 possessed the suit land and the plain- tiff by the so-called purchase from defendant Nos. 44-60 got possession in the suit land.

III. Admittedly, the suit land was not recorded in the name of predecessor of the plaintiff in the records of right and there is no evidence that they ever paid rent for the suit land.

IV. The plaintiff's witnesses could not prove his possession or the alleged possession of his predecessor in the suit land.

V. Defendant-respondent Nos. 3-22 by filing several suits obtained decrees in respect of the suit land and, as such, they acquired title to and possession in the suit land.

34. Mr Parimal Chandra Guha, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent Nos. 46 and 47, submitted that though respondent Nos. 46 and claimed to have possession in certain portion of the suit land, they have no document in support of their title in the suit land.

35. I have gone through the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division and the materials on record.

36. Admittedly Gonga Charan was the CS recorded owner of the suit land. According to the plaintiff, Gonga Charan settled the suit land to Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader by a registered patta dated 24-3-1936 who transferred their under tenancy interest by a registered deed of sale dated 27-8-1943 to Burundi Hawlader, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 44-60. Burundi Hawlader died leaving behind defendant Nos. 44-60 as his heirs and they transferred 5.08 acres of land (suit land) out of 6.05 acres of land by a registered deed of sale dated 28-1-1993 to the plaintiff. The contesting defendants claimed that for arrear of rents, the suit land was sold in auction and Shashi Kumar Singh purchased the same on 17-11-1941 and subsequently, Shashi Kumar Singh settled the suit land along with other lands to the predecessor-in-interest of the contesting defendants. To prove their case, the contesting defendants filed sale certificate marked as Exhibit-6. The alleged sale certificate has not been substantiated by any sale proclamation and writ of delivery of possession. A sale certificate is not conclusive but only prima facie evidence of title and it can be shown that it is wrong and relates to property, which was not sold.

37. Having gone through the sale certificate (Exhibit-6), it appears that the Gonga Charan was the judgment-debtor. Admittedly, GongaCharan created under tenancy by a registered patta dated 24-3-1936 in favour of Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader. A certified copy of the said patta was marked Exhibit-5 without any objection. Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader sold their under tenancy interest to Burundi Hawlader by a registered deed of sale dated 27-8-1943. A certified copy of the said deed was marked as Exhibit-5ka without any objection. Therefore, even if, the superior interest of Gonga Charan was sold in auction, there is nothing on record to show that Shashi Kumar Singh annulled the under tenancy created by Gonga Charan according to the provision of 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The contesting defendants in their written statement did not state anything about annulment of the under tenancy created by Gonga Charan in favour of Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader, who sold their under tenancy interest to Burundi Hawlader. The plaintiff could prove that the registered patta dated 24-3-1936 (Exhibit-5) and the registered deed of sale dated 27-8-1943 (Exhibit-5ka) by bringing the volumes from the Office of the Sub-Registrar through PW 6, Md Matab Ali Hawlader, a permanent Mohararof Khulna Sub-Registry Office. The contesting defendant respondent Nos. 3-22 did not challenge those documents. Unless the under tenancy is annulled it shall be deemed that Burundi Hawlader and subsequently his heirs continued in possession of 6.05 acres of land It is contended that the registered patta dated 24-3- 1936 and the deed of sale dated 27.08.1943 were not acted upon. According to the Registration Act, title passes to the transferee as soon as the registration of a deed is completed. So the above contention falls through.

38. Ar as per the CS Khatian No. 153 (Exhibit-C), the registered patta dated 24.03 1936 and the registered deed of sale dated 27-8-1943 (exhihit-5ka), the of CS Plot No. 3427 was canal (খালবিলান), CS Plot No. 2328 was raised land (ডাংগা)and CS Plot No. 3429 was homestead (ডাংগা)having four dwelling huts. From those Exhibits, it appears that the under tenancy was not created in respect of null land.

39. Section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act provides for 'protected interests'. Clause-C of section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act runs as under:

"160. Protected interests.-The following shall be deemed to be protected interests within the meaning of this Chapter:-

(a) ……………………

(b)…………………….

(c) any lease of land whereon dwelling houses, manufactories or other permanent buildings have been erected, or permanent gardens, plantations, tanks canals, places of worship of burning or burying grounds have been made;

(d………………….

(e) ………………..

(f) ……………….

(ff) ……………….

(g) …………………”

40. Having considered clause-C of section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, it appears that the under tenancy created by Gonga Charan Hawlader in favour of Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader was projected under the clause mentioned above. The under tenancy holders transferred their under tenancy right to Burundi Hawlader by a registered deed of sale dated 27-8-1943 and, as such, the under tenancy purchased by Burundi Hawlader is also protected interest under clause-(C) of section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act.

41. Section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act deals with annulment of incumbrances. Sub-section 4 of section 167 runs as follows:

"(4) when a tenure, of holding is sold in execution of a decree or a certificate signed under the Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 for arrears due in respect thereof, and there is on the tenure or holding a protected interest of the kind specified in section 160, clause (c) the purchaser may, if he has power under this Chapter or that Act to avoid all incumbrances, sue to enhance the rent of the land which is the subject of the protected interest. On proof that the land is held at a rent which was not at the time the lease was granted a fair rent, the Court may enhance the rent, to such amount as appears to be fair and equitable. "

<u>42. Having considered sub-section 4 of section 167, it appears that in respect of protected interests as contained in clause-(c) of section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act the auction purchaser could sue for enhancement of rent but could not evict the under tenant when the nature of land comes within c\ause-3 of section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Having considered clause- (3) of section 160 and sub-section 4 of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, I am of the opinion that Burundi Hawlader could not be evicted by the auction purchaser Shashi Kumar Singh pursuant to the sale certificate (Exhibit-6). Shashi Kumar Singh only purchased the superior interest of Gonga Charan Hawlader and he was entitled to receive rent from the heirs of Burundi Hawlader.</u>

43. In the light of discussion made before, there can be no shadow of doubt that the plaintiff by his purchase dated 28-1-1993 from Burundi Hawlader acquired valid title in the suit land.

<u>44. The contesting defendants claimed that Shashi Kumar Singh died leaving behind two sons, namely, Kanai Lal Singh and HiraLal Singh. The contesting defendants brought Title Suit No. 173 of 1964 in the Court of the then Subordinate Judge, Khulna against Kanai Lal Singh and HiraLal Singh and the suit was stated to have been decreed on compromise on 8-9-1964. The contesting defendants also stated that they brought Title Suit No. 109 of 1971 in the Court of the then Subordinate Judge, Khulna for declaration of their title and for further declaration that enlistment of the suit land in the list of vested and non-resident property was void and obtained ex-parte decree on 15-6-1972. The contesting defendants also brought Title Suit No. 207 if 1978 in the First Court of Munsif, Bagherhat for permanent injunction and obtained ex-parte decree on 20-12-1980. Against the ex-parte decree, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Bagherhat and Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Sharonkhula, brought Title Suit No. 33 of 1985 for setting aside the said ex-parte decree and the Suit was dismissed on 8-6-1990. Admittedly, the heirs of Burundi Hawlader were not made parties in those suits and the compromise and the ex-parte decree were obtained behind their back and, as such, neither the heirs of Burundi Hawlader nor the plaintiff was at all bound by those decrees. The contesting defendants in order to grab the suit land managed to obtain a compromise decree in Title Suit No. 173 of 1964, ex-parte decrees in Title Suit No.109 of 1971 and in Title Suit No. 20 of 1978. When the contesting defendants failed to prove their title in the suit land these decrees cannot confer title on them, in which, the heirs of Burundi were not made parties.</u>

<u>45. The High Court Division came to the finding that the suit filed by the plaintiff was barred by limitation. It is well settled that if the plaintiff comes with a suit for declaration that the entry made in the record right is wrong, in that case Article 102 of the Limitation Act will be applicable, but the plaintiff is not bound to institute a suit for declaration that the entry is wrong. He can wait and when an invasion on his right is made on the basis of the entry, he can sue for declaration of his title on the ground that the record is wrong and, as such, a suit will be in time if brought within six years from the date of threatened invasion. Having considered the materials on record, I find that the plaintiff's suit is not barred by limitation as he filed the suit when his right was denied in the suit land by the contesting defendants. Mere non recording the name of Burundi Hawlader or the names of his heirs in the khatians or nor payment of rent could not extinguish the title of Burundi Hawlader and his heirs and the plaintiff by his subsequent purchases from the heirs of Burundi Hawlader acquired valid title in the suit land.</u>

46. Admittedly, the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title simpliciter without any prayer for recovery of possession. Had the plaintiff not in possession of 5.05 acres of land as contained in Exhibit-l dated 28-1-1993 he would have brought a suit not only for declaration of title but also for recovery of khash possession.

47. Now it is to be seen whether the plaintiff could prove his possession in the suit land PW 1, Shaheen Reza, the plaintiff in his evidence stated that he purchased the suit land on 28-1-1993 and that after purchase he went into possession of the suit land. The contesting defendants could not discredit his evidence in respect of possession of the suit land. PW 2, Abdus Sattar Jamader, aged about 65 years in his evidence stated that he knew the suit land because he had land adjacent to the suit land. He further stated that plaintiff had been in possession of the suit land. He knew Nittananda Hawlader and they purchased the suit land and Burundi Hawlader possessed the suit land. The plaintiff had been possessing the suit land after his purchase from the heirs of Burundi Hawlader. PW 3, Abdul Khaleque Talukder in his evidence stated that he knew the suit land and that his house was adjacent to the suit land. He knew Ananta Kumar Dey and Nittananda Hawlader and the plaintiff possessed the suit land and he never saw the defendants possessing the suit land. This witness in cross-examination stated that the suit land is three miles away from the house of the defendants. PW 4, Nurul Haque Talukder, aged about 75 years, in his evidence, stated that he knew the suit land and that he had land adjacent to the suit land and that his daughter lived there. The plaintiff now possessed the suit land. He married the plaintiff's brother's daughter. PW 5 Abdul Hakim Akhando, aged about 54/55 years, in his evidence, stated that he inherited the suit land from his mother. They sold the suit land to the plaintiff by a registered deed of sale dated 21-3-1993 and he was present at the time of registration of the kabala. He stated that there were 2/3 dwelling houses in the big plot of the suit land. PW 6, Md Matab Ali Hawlader, a permanent Moharer of Khulna Sub-Registry Office, in his evidence stated that he brought the volumes containing the registered patta dated 24-2-1936 and the deed of sale dated 27-8-1943.

48. DW 1 Muslem Farazee, defendant No.7, aged about 45 years, stated that 6.14 acres of land of CS Khatian belonged to Gonga Charan and that the said land was sold in auction in Rent Case No. 908 of 1941. Shashi Kumar Singh purchased the said land of the said khatian in auction and Shashi Kumar Singh went into possession on 17.11.1941. Shashi Kumar Singh settled the suit land along with other lands measuring 16.93 acres to their predecessors and his paternal uncle in 14A.1948. In cross-examination, this witness stated that he could produce paper in support of the settlement. In this connection, it is pertinent to note the contesting defendants could not produce any scrap of paper in support of their settlement. This witness, however, stated that they had been in possession of the suit land. The contesting defendants examine only DW 2 in support of their case. DW 2 stated that he knew the plaintiff and the defendants and the suit land. He used to cultivate the suit land by taking barga from Latiff and Sharif and others and that he had been cultivating the suit land for the last two years. DW 3 was examined on behalf of defendant Nos. 37-41 (Government). The name of this witness is Tarun Kumar Dutta. He is an Office Assistant in Sharonkhula Police Station VP Office, and he deposed that the suit land has been recorded as vested property and that it was leased out to lessees. Neither the plaintiff nor the con- testing defendants had possession in the suit land and the Government possessed the suit land.

<u>49. The plaintiff examined 6 witnesses including himself. PWs 2, 3, 4 and 5 proved the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. PW 3 in his cross-examination stated that the suit land is three miles away from the house of the contesting defendant-respondent Nos. 3-22. On the other hand, defendant Nos. 3-22 examined only 2 witnesses including defendant No. 7 and both the witnesses miserably failed to prove the possession of contesting defendant-respondent Nos. 3-22 in the suit land. When evidence is adduced by both the parties the question of onus becomes immaterial. The plaintiff succeeded in proving his possession by examining PWs. 2, 3, 4, and 5. The contesting defendant-respondent examined only 2 DWs apart from defendant No.7 who was examined as DW 1 and they miserably failed to prove possession of defendant-respondent Nos. 3-22.</u>

50. I have already found the plaintiff acquired valid title in the suit land and there is an age-old maxim 'Title follows possession'. In the light of the findings made before, I am of the opinion that the plaintiff had been able to prove his title to and possession in the suit land. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the judgment delivered by the High court Division is set aside.

This appeal is dismissed by majority decision.
